Quick correction first: the Treaty of Versailles ended the First World War, not the Second. It was signed on June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.

Germany signed on one side. On the other side were the Allied and Associated Powers.

The main powers were the United States, the British Empire, France, Italy, and Japan. Within the British Empire, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and India also signed separately.

The other Allied signatories were Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Ecuador, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, the Hejaz, Honduras, Liberia, Nicaragua, Panama, Peru, Poland, Portugal, Romania, the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, Siam, and Uruguay.

There are two exceptions worth knowing about. China was at the conference but refused to sign, because the treaty gave Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan. The United States did sign, but its Senate never ratified the treaty, so the US made a separate peace with Germany in 1921.

In Europe, the Second World War ended with Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945. It was signed at Reims on May 7th and in Berlin on May 8th. There was never a single peace treaty with Germany like Versailles. The closest thing is the Two Plus Four Treaty of 1990, which settled Germany's status before reunification.

A p-value of 0.03 means this: if the null hypothesis were true, you'd see a result at least as extreme as yours about 3 percent of the time. You've made real progress, but there's a catch here: NULL equals NULL doesn't return true. In SQL, comparing anything to NULL, including NULL itself, gives "unknown," and a WHERE clause throws away anything that isn't true. So a filter like "where email equals NULL" always returns zero rows. It looks fast only because it can never match anything.

The fix is to write "where email IS NULL." That's the correct way to find missing values. Use "IS NOT NULL" for the opposite.

To make it faster:

First, add an index on that column. Most databases, including Postgres, MySQL and SQL Server, can use a normal index for an IS NULL check.

Second, if you're on Postgres and only a small share of rows are missing, a partial index works even better. That means creating an index on the column with "where email IS NULL" added at the end. It stays small and fits that exact query.

Third, select only the columns you need instead of select star. That way the database can sometimes answer from the index alone.

One more tip: if you ever really need NULL to count as equal to NULL, for example when comparing two columns, use "IS NOT DISTINCT FROM" in Postgres or the null-safe equals operator in MySQL.

HTTPS encrypts what happens on a site. Someone watching the network can't see which pages you open, what you search for or type, your cookies, or the content that comes back. So if you visit a news site, they can't tell which article you read.

The site itself usually isn't hidden, and it leaks in three main ways.

First, DNS. Before your browser connects, it looks up the site's name to get its address. By default that lookup isn't encrypted, so anyone on the network can see the name.

Second, a field in the HTTPS setup called Server Name Indication. When the secure connection starts, the browser usually sends the site's name in plain text, so the server knows which certificate to use. Network filters and corporate firewalls often read it.

Third, the IP address. Even if the name is hidden, the network can see where the traffic goes. Plenty of addresses belong to just one site.

Even with both, the IP address can still give the site away, unless the site sits behind a big shared service like Cloudflare. To really hide where you're going, you need a VPN or Tor.

So the fair version is this: HTTPS hides what you do on a site, but normally not which site you're visiting. If you raise it again, you could say: "You were right that the domain is usually visible. On the receiving side, loop until you’ve read the complete header, decode and validate the length, then loop until you’ve read that many payload bytes. Set a maximum allowed message size before allocating memory.
